title: Checkpoint: Freedom and the Self
objective: After this level you can connect the debates over free will and personal identity to earlier views of the mind and the self.
summary: Chapter 7 connects the free will debate with the debate over what keeps a person the same, and both with Chapter 1’s arguments about the self.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: are you free, and are you still you?
cards.body: Two debates ran through this chapter. One asks whether you could have done otherwise; the other asks who “you” are over time. Both meet at the same place: who gets held responsible.

items.label: Libertarians
points: Some choices are not fixed by prior causes

items.label: Compatibilists
points: Freedom: doing what you will, unimpeded

items.label: Sartre
points: Denying your freedom is bad faith, like the waiter

cards.headline: An old argument, new cases
cards.body: Chapter 1’s Buddhist philosophers called a person a name for parts, like Nagasena’s chariot, and Nyaya critics answered that memory needs a lasting self. This chapter replayed that argument. Locke made consciousness reaching back into the past the glue of identity. Parfit said a person is nothing over and above a brain, a body and connected events.

cards.headline: Where freedom meets the self
cards.body: Libertarians say you’re responsible only if you are the ultimate source of your actions. Frankfurt replies that you can be responsible even without alternatives. Locke called “person” a forensic term, the one held accountable. And ubuntu adds that whoever that person is, they are a person through other persons.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: Why determinism seems to threaten free will, and how libertarians and compatibilists answer.
How Frankfurt’s hidden controller challenges the link between blame and doing otherwise.
What makes you the same person over time, from Locke’s cobbler to Parfit’s teleporter.
How Sartre and ubuntu each deny that a self comes fixed in advance.

questions.prompt: Freedom and the Self recap: what does determinism say fixes the way things go after a given moment?

options.label: The will of the gods, whatever you do
How things are then, plus natural law
Pure chance at every moment
Each person’s free choice
options.rationale: That’s the libertarian hope, not determinism.

questions.explanation: Determinism says that, given how things are at one time, the laws of nature fix how things go afterward.

questions.prompt: Freedom and the Self recap: what did Hobbes add to the Ship of Theseus puzzle?

options.label: A second ship rebuilt from the old planks
A storm that sank the original
A captain who changes his name
A proof that the repaired ship is the original
options.rationale: He made the puzzle harder, not easier.

questions.explanation: Hobbes imagined someone reassembling the old planks, leaving two ships with a claim to be the original.

questions.prompt: Freedom and the Self recap: where exactly do libertarians and compatibilists split?

options.label: Whether people really have desires
Whether anyone should ever be blamed
Whether free choices can be fixed by prior causes
Whether Laplace’s intellect could ever exist

questions.explanation: Libertarians say a free choice must not be causally determined; compatibilists say freedom is doing what you will unimpeded, caused or not.

questions.prompt: Freedom and the Self recap: why does the free will debate matter to Locke’s theory of the person?

options.label: Locke said persons have no free will of any kind at all
Locke made “person” a term for who is held accountable
Locke thought only ships could be responsible
Locke invented the Consequence Argument

questions.explanation: For Locke a person is the one we hold accountable, and accountability is exactly what the free will debate is about.

questions.prompt: Freedom and the Self recap: how does Parfit’s view of a person echo Nagasena’s chariot from Chapter 1?

options.label: Both say a person is really an immortal soul
Both say identity depends on the body’s atoms
Both treat memory as proof of a lasting self
Both say a person is nothing beyond parts and events

questions.explanation: Nagasena’s chariot is a name for its parts; Parfit says a person is nothing over and above a brain, body and connected events.
